Dear Keerthana,
You asked what I've been up to since I stopped answering 'how are you' with 'fine.' Here's the honest version.
In January my boss said I seemed 'checked out,' and I realised I couldn't even tell her what I was feeling. So I started small. I printed a page of emotion words and stuck it inside my wardrobe door. Every night I write two lines: what my body did today, and which word might fit. 'Jaw clenched on the bus: annoyed?' 'Heavy shoulders after Amma's call: guilty? tired?'
In March, when it still felt tangled, I booked a counsellor. Best decision.
So, to answer your question properly: today I feel hopeful. And a little shy telling you this.
Love,
Ayesha

Week one. Jahnavi, his sister, had asked Akash why he never said how he felt, and he couldn't answer. So he downloaded a feelings chart and stuck it inside his wardrobe. Most words looked the same to him. The only thing he could write in his phone notes that night was: "Chest tight before meeting."
Week three. At his second session, the counsellor asked what the tight chest might be. Akash stared at the chart printout. "Nervous? No. Scared I'll look stupid." He was surprised by how right it felt.
Week seven. Sunday lunch at their parents' flat. Everyone was planning Jahnavi's engagement, and nobody had asked him anything. Akash put his fork down. "I feel left out," he said. "I'd like to help with something."
Jahnavi stared at him, then grinned. "Who are you, and what have you done with my brother?" She handed him the guest list.

Elizabeth, you said your fiancé never tells you what he feels. Let me tell you a story about a man who couldn't.
I was twenty-five, newly married. My wife would ask, "What's wrong?" and I'd say "Nothing." And I believed it. I only knew my chest was tight or my jaw hurt. I thought I was just tired.
One day she cried and said, "It's like living with a wall." That scared me.
So I started, awkwardly. I wrote feeling words on a sheet and stuck it inside my cupboard. Every night I wrote two lines: what my body felt, what word might fit. "Chest tight. Nervous? Angry?" When it still felt like shouting in a dark room, I went to a counsellor, which in those days took some courage.
I'm Lalit, and it took two years. But my wife says I talk too much now.

qa.q: Where did Lalit stick the sheet of feeling words?
qa.a: Inside the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when his wife said "It's like living with a wall"?
qa.a: He felt scared and shaken, realising his silence was hurting her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Lalit's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Starting the list of words and nightly notes, then seeing a counsellor when it was still hard, was the turning point, because it built his words step by step with support.

qa.q: How might Lalit's wife have felt during those two years?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely at first, then hopeful as he slowly started talking more.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young adult, he built a feeling-word list, noticed body cues, wrote notes and saw a counsellor.

Last year my manager called me "unreadable" in my appraisal. My friend Ujjwal said I answered every question with "it's okay". I, Tanvir, honestly didn't know what else to say. Inside there was only a kind of noise.
In March I went to a counsellor because I'd been snapping at my team and couldn't sleep. She didn't push. She gave me a wheel of feeling words and asked me to notice where things landed in my body.
So now I keep a small notebook. Tight jaw usually means frustrated. Hot neck means embarrassed. A hollow stomach, I'm learning, is lonely.
It is slow. Some days I write only "bad". But last week I told Ujjwal, "I felt left out when you didn't invite me," and he apologised. That sentence took me a year.

She says Nilesh now asks, "What's the word today?" and she can answer more often than not. We will continue fortnightly.

qa.a: The feeling-word list, the body map and the daily notes, which help Zeenat move from 'off' and a tight chest to words like humiliated and disappointed.
